text-input.what: A single-line box where people type short text such as a name, email address or code.
uses: Collecting names, email addresses and phone numbers.
Entering short codes, usernames or search terms.
Capturing numbers with units, such as a port or a postcode.
avoid: Long answers: use a multi-line text area instead.
A small set of known options: use radio buttons or a select.
practices: Give every field a visible label, not just placeholder text.
Set the right input type so phones show a suitable keyboard.
Turn on autofill hints for common details like name and email.
Size the box to the expected answer length.
Explain errors next to the field and say how to fix them.

textarea.what: A multi-line box for longer free text such as notes, messages or descriptions. It grows or scrolls as people type.
uses: Comments, feedback and support messages.
Descriptions and notes on a record.
Pasting in longer text, such as an address list.
avoid: Short one-line answers: use a text input.
Rich formatting needs: use a rich text editor.
practices: Make the box tall enough to show that a longer answer is expected.
State any character limit and show a live count.
Keep a visible label above the box.
Let people resize it vertically when the layout allows.

select.what: A dropdown menu that lets people pick one option from a list. It saves space when the list is fairly long.
uses: Choosing a country, state or time zone.
Picking one value from a medium list where space is tight.
Sorting or filtering by a single category.
avoid: Very few options: radio buttons show all choices without a click.
Long lists people know by name: use a search field with suggestions.
practices: Keep options in a meaningful order, such as alphabetical or by frequency.
Start with a clear prompt like 'Choose an option' when no default fits.
Group long lists under headings.
Prefer the browser's own dropdown, especially on phones.

listbox.what: A list that shows several options at once and lets people select one or more. It is a plain form control with a visible list.
uses: Picking several items from a short list in a dense admin screen.
Assigning multiple tags or roles to a record.
Choosing items where seeing all options at once helps.
avoid: Most public forms: a group of checkboxes is easier to understand.
Long lists: use a search field with multi-select suggestions.
practices: Tell people how to select more than one item.
Show enough rows to see most options without scrolling.
Label the list clearly and keep options short.
Make sure it works with the keyboard alone.

search-input.what: A text field made for searching, usually with a magnifier icon and a button to clear what was typed.
uses: Searching a whole site or app.
Filtering a long list or table.
Finding a person, product or document by name.
avoid: Choosing from a short, fixed list: use a select or radio buttons.
Browsing by category: use navigation or filters.
practices: Use the familiar magnifier icon.
Give the field an accessible name even when there is no visible label.
Let people clear the text in one tap.
Show results quickly and say clearly when nothing matches.

checkbox.what: A small box that people tick or untick. It records a yes or no, or lets people pick any number of options.
uses: Agreeing to terms or opting in to emails.
Selecting several options in a form that is submitted.
Selecting rows in a list or table.
avoid: Settings that apply instantly: use a switch.
Choosing exactly one option: use radio buttons.
practices: Make the whole label clickable, not just the box.
Word labels positively so ticking means yes.
Group related checkboxes under a clear heading.
Never pre-tick boxes that help the business more than the user.

radio.what: A round button used in a group where only one option can be chosen at a time.
uses: Choosing one plan, shipping method or payment type.
Answering a question with a few clear options.
Options that need a short description each.
avoid: Many options: use a select or a search field.
A single yes or no: use a checkbox or switch.
practices: List the options vertically so they are easy to compare.
Put the group under a clear question or heading.
Pre-select an option only if it is a sensible default.
Make the whole label clickable.

switch.what: A toggle that turns a setting on or off and takes effect right away, like a physical light switch.
uses: Turning notifications or autoplay on and off.
Enabling a feature in a settings page.
Settings that save immediately without a Save button.
avoid: Forms that are submitted with a button: use a checkbox.
Choosing between more than two options: use radio buttons.
practices: Apply the change immediately and confirm it happened.
Label the setting itself, not the action.
Show the on and off states with more than colour alone.
Undo the change and explain if saving fails.

number-input.what: A field for entering a number, often with plus and minus buttons for small changes.
uses: Setting quantities, counts or limits.
Adjusting a value up or down by small steps.
Entering amounts with a minimum and maximum.
avoid: Identifiers like phone, card or postcode numbers: use a text input with a numeric keyboard.
Wide ranges: use a slider or plain typing.
practices: Set sensible minimum, maximum and step values.
Show the unit in the label or beside the field.
Let people type as well as use the buttons.
Name the buttons so screen readers say what they change.

color-input.what: A control for picking a colour, usually a swatch that opens a picker plus a text box for the exact colour code.
uses: Choosing a theme or brand colour.
Labelling categories, calendars or zones with a colour.
Setting a colour in a drawing or design tool.
avoid: Picking from a few set colours: use radio buttons with swatches.
Colour is the only way to tell options apart: add text or icons.
practices: Show the current colour and its code together.
Accept codes with or without the hash and in any case.
Warn when a colour is hard to read against text.
Offer a few preset colours for quick picks.

file-input.what: A control that lets people choose a file from their device to upload, such as a photo or document.
uses: Uploading photos, avatars or scans.
Attaching documents to a form or message.
Importing a data file such as a spreadsheet.
avoid: Files already stored online: let people paste a link or pick from a library.
Typing short text: use a text input.
practices: Say which file types and sizes are allowed before people choose.
Check the file again on the server.
Show the chosen file name and a way to remove it.
Allow several files only when you can handle them.

otp-digit.what: A row of single-digit boxes for entering a one-time code, such as a text-message or email verification code.
uses: Two-step sign-in codes.
Email or phone number verification.
Confirming a sensitive action with a short code.
avoid: Codes with letters or more than 8 characters: use one text field.
Long-term passwords: use a password field.
practices: Move to the next box automatically after each digit.
Let people paste the whole code at once.
Allow phones to fill the code from a text message.
Use a numeric keyboard on phones.
Offer a way to resend the code.

input-addon.what: A fixed piece of text or a button attached to the side of an input, such as a unit, a currency sign or a Copy button.
uses: Showing a unit like minutes, percent or metres.
Adding a fixed prefix like https:// or a currency sign.
Attaching an action such as Copy or Test.
avoid: Long explanations: put them in help text under the field.
Actions unrelated to the field: use a separate button.
practices: Keep the addon text very short.
Make clear the addon is not part of what people type.
Connect the addon text to the input for screen readers.
Make sure attached buttons are large enough to tap.

day-cell.what: One day in a month calendar. It shows the date number and a few events for that day.
uses: Showing a month of days in a grid.
Marking today, weekends and holidays.
Giving a quick view of what is on each day.
avoid: Detailed schedules with times: use a week or day view.
Long lists of events: use an agenda list.
practices: Mark today clearly and not by colour alone.
Limit visible events and link to the rest.
Make the day number a link to the day view.
Keep cell heights equal so weeks line up.

week-header.what: A heading for a week view that shows the week number and the dates it covers.
uses: Titling a week view or weekly planner.
Roster and sprint pages that plan by week.
Showing which dates a week covers.
avoid: Month views: use a month heading.
Single-day views: show the full date instead.
practices: Show both the week number and the date range.
Include the year when the range crosses a year end.
Use the local way of numbering weeks.
Mark dates with a proper date format for assistive tools.

weekday-header.what: The row of day names, such as Mon to Sun, above the columns of a calendar grid.
uses: Labelling columns in a month or week calendar.
Showing which days are weekends.
Date pickers and booking grids.
avoid: Views where each row is a day: label the rows with full dates.
practices: Start the week on the day people in that region expect.
Use short names, with the full name available to screen readers.
Set the weekend apart without relying on colour alone.
Mark them as column headers for assistive tools.

week-row.what: One row of a month calendar covering seven days, often with its week number at the start.
uses: Building a month grid from week by week.
Showing week numbers beside each row.
Grouping days so the month is easier to scan.
avoid: Week views with hours: use hour rows and day columns.
practices: Always show exactly seven days per row.
Show week numbers only if people plan by week.
Mark the row's week number as a row header.
Keep rows equal in height.

hour-row.what: One hour of a day or week schedule, with a time label and space for events.
uses: Day and week views with a time scale.
Resource and room schedulers.
Booking tools that show free and busy times.
avoid: Month views, where days are too small for hours.
Short lists of events: use an agenda list.
practices: Show working hours first and scroll to the current time.
Keep the lines faint so events stand out.
Use the same hour height across the whole view.
Use a 12 or 24 hour clock that matches local habits.

time-slot.what: A block of time, often half an hour, in a schedule. People pick it to book or add an event.
uses: Booking an appointment at a free time.
Adding an event by clicking where it should go.
Showing which times are free or busy.
avoid: Picking a date only: use a date picker.
Long events: show them as event blocks across the slots.
practices: Make every free slot large enough to tap.
Show busy and selected slots without relying on colour alone.
Name each slot with its date and time for screen readers.
Reveal hints on hover or focus to keep the grid calm.

all-day-row.what: A strip at the top of a day or week calendar for events that last all day or span several days.
uses: Holidays, birthdays and day-long events.
Trips and multi-day events across columns.
Keeping all-day items apart from timed events.
avoid: Events with a start and end time: place them in the hour grid.
practices: Keep it above the timed hours.
Stretch multi-day events across the days they cover.
Show when an event continues past the visible days.
Label the row clearly, for example 'All day'.

event-chip.what: A small one-line label for an event, usually with a colour dot, a time and a title. It fits in a tight space.
uses: Showing events inside month calendar cells.
Compact lists of events.
Linking a short entry to its full details.
avoid: Roomy views: use an event card with more detail.
Long lists: use an agenda list.
practices: Show the start time and the first words of the title.
Use a dot to show which calendar it belongs to.
Give each chip a full spoken name.
Mark cancelled events with more than colour alone.

event-card.what: A block that represents an event in a day or week calendar, showing its title, time and place.
uses: Showing events in day and week views.
Opening the details of an event.
Showing how long events last.
avoid: Crowded month cells: use small chips.
Simple lists: use an agenda item.
practices: Size each block to the event's length.
Show title first, then time and place.
Mark tentative events with a pattern, not colour alone.
Keep text readable against the card colour.
Let overlapping events share the width.

agenda-item.what: One entry in a list of events, usually with the time on the left and the title and details beside it.
uses: Upcoming event lists.
Calendars on small phone screens.
A day's schedule in text form.
avoid: Seeing free and busy gaps at a glance: use a day or week grid.
practices: Group events under day headings.
Put all-day events first.
Keep the time in a fixed column so it is easy to scan.
Show only the details people need, such as place.

date-badge.what: A small box that looks like a calendar page, showing the month, day number and weekday.
uses: Marking dates beside events in a list.
Showing deadlines and upcoming dates.
Headings for each day in an agenda.
avoid: Dates in running text: write the date in words.
Dates with times: show the time too.
practices: Keep it small and consistent in every list.
Give screen readers the full date in words.
Use the real date tag for assistive tools.
Do not rely on colour to carry meaning.

holiday-label.what: A short label naming a public holiday or closure on a calendar day.
uses: Marking public holidays in a month view.
Explaining why a site or office is closed.
Showing closures in schedules.
avoid: Personal events: use an event chip.
Normal working days: show nothing extra.
practices: Use the holiday's name, not just a colour.
Add a mark or pattern so it is not colour-only.
Say clearly when the place is closed.
Keep the label short enough to fit the cell.

more-events-link.what: A short link such as '+3 more' that shows when a calendar day has more events than fit.
uses: Crowded cells in a month calendar.
Opening the full list of one day.
Showing that events are hidden, not missing.
avoid: Days with space: show all events directly.
practices: Show the exact number of hidden events.
Open a popover or the day view with the full list.
Give the link a spoken name that includes the date.
Make it big enough to tap on phones.

calendar-header.what: The top bar of a calendar with the current month or period, arrows to move, and a switch between views.
uses: Showing which period is on screen.
Moving to the previous or next month or week.
Switching between day, week, month and agenda views.
avoid: Date pickers inside forms: use a compact picker header.
practices: Show the period in words, such as 'November 2026'.
Include a Today button to jump back.
Name the arrows for screen readers.
Keep the controls in the same place in every view.

vertical-stack.what: A layout that places sections one under another with even gaps between them.
uses: The main column of a page.
Sections inside a side panel.
Forms and settings pages with several groups.
avoid: Side-by-side content: use a grid or a split layout.
practices: Use one consistent gap between sections.
Make gaps between sections larger than gaps inside them.
Control spacing from the parent, not each child.
Keep a logical reading order.

stat-grid.what: A grid of small cards each showing one key number, arranged in equal columns that wrap on small screens.
uses: Headline numbers at the top of a dashboard.
Summaries at the top of a record or report.
Comparing a few key figures at a glance.
avoid: Many details per metric: use a table or chart.
More than about six numbers: pick the ones that matter.
practices: Keep cards the same size so numbers are easy to compare.
Limit the grid to 3 to 6 cards.
Let cards wrap on narrow screens.
Label every number clearly with its unit.

card-grid-layout.what: A layout that arranges cards in as many equal columns as fit the screen, from one column on phones to several on wide screens.
uses: Browsing videos, products, people or plans.
Collections scanned by picture or title.
Dashboards of similar items.
avoid: Comparing items across many attributes: use a table.
Long text: use a single-column list.
practices: Give every card the same shape.
Set a minimum card width so text stays readable.
Keep gaps even in both directions.
Keep the order logical for keyboard and screen readers.

two-column-grid.what: A layout with two equal columns that stack into one on narrow screens.
uses: Pairing two charts or lists of equal weight.
Side-by-side comparisons.
Dashboards with two panels per row.
avoid: Main content with a side note: use a main and aside split.
Three or more items: use a card grid.
practices: Use it only for content of equal importance.
Make sure the stacked order reads well on phones.
Keep both columns similar in height.
Keep the gap between columns consistent.

split-layout.what: A page layout with a wide main column and a narrower side column beside it. The side column drops below on small screens.
uses: A form with help or summary beside it.
A record with related items.
A booking page with an order summary.
avoid: Content of equal weight: use two equal columns.
Long forms: use a single narrow column.
practices: Put the main content first in the source order.
Keep the aside for secondary information only.
Move the aside below the main content on narrow screens.
Do not hide vital content in the aside.

media-split.what: A layout that shows a large picture or video beside its details and controls. The media stays in view while the rest scrolls.
uses: Video, camera or recording pages.
Image editors with settings.
Maps or previews next to their options.
avoid: Pages with little media: use a main and aside split.
Small screens: stack the media above the details.
practices: Keep the media visible while people adjust settings.
Give the media about two thirds of the width.
Stack the media first on phones.
Reserve the media's space so the page does not jump.

form-grid.what: A form layout that puts short related fields side by side and lets long fields use the full width.
uses: Settings pages with many short fields.
Address and connection details.
Pairs such as host and port or from and to.
avoid: Ordinary forms: one column is easier to follow.
Long answers: give them the full width.
practices: Only pair fields that belong together.
Let long fields such as notes span the full width.
Keep the reading order logical when the grid collapses.
Keep labels above their fields.

narrow-form.what: A form layout with a single column of fields that is kept narrow so lines are short and easy to follow.
uses: Sign-up, login and contact forms.
Create and edit pages.
Settings forms.
avoid: Forms with many short related fields: consider a form grid.
Wide data entry like tables: use a full-width layout.
practices: Put fields in one column, top to bottom.
Keep the form around 36rem wide or less.
Group related fields under clear headings.
Put the main action at the end of the form.

product-grid.what: A grid of product tiles, each with a picture, name and price. The number of columns adapts to the screen.
uses: Online shop and catalogue listings.
Category and search results pages.
Browsing items by picture.
avoid: Comparing many specifications: use a table.
A single product: use a product page.
practices: Keep tiles the same size and shape.
Show price and name consistently.
Use pagination or load more below the grid.
Put sorting and filtering above the grid.
Give every image a useful text alternative or an empty one if decorative.

video-grid.what: A grid of video cards showing a preview image, name and status for each video or camera.
uses: Dashboards of cameras or video streams.
Video libraries in card view.
Showing which videos are live or offline.
avoid: Comparing many details: use a table.
Watching one stream closely: use a full player.
practices: Show important items such as pinned videos first.
Mark offline items with text and a badge, not colour alone.
Reserve the image space so the page does not jump.
Show a placeholder while previews load.

kpi-grid.what: A row of cards showing the most important numbers, each often with a change over time and a link to details.
uses: The top of a dashboard or report.
A quick health check of a system or business.
Linking key numbers to deeper pages.
avoid: Detailed analysis: use charts and tables.
More than about six metrics: pick the ones people act on.
practices: Show only a few numbers that matter.
Add a comparison, such as change since last week.
Label every number with a clear name and unit.
Link each card to its source.

capacity-heat-map.what: A table of shaded cells showing how busy something is across days and hours. Darker cells mean higher values.
uses: Spotting the busiest hours of a venue.
Planning staff and opening hours.
Finding patterns in activity over a week.
avoid: Exact comparisons of a few values: use a table or bar chart.
Trends over time: use a line chart.
practices: Print the value in each cell so it does not depend on colour.
Show a legend explaining the scale.
Use one colour in graded steps.
Mark missing data differently from low values.

event-timeline.what: A list of events in time order, grouped by day, with markers showing the sequence and type of each event.
uses: Alert and activity histories.
Audit logs and incident reviews.
The history of a single item.
avoid: Comparing many events by detail: use a table.
Future plans: use a calendar or agenda.
practices: Group by day with clear day headings.
Show the newest first unless the story reads better in order.
Use text as well as colour for status.
Show the time for each event.
Link each entry to its details.
